content: The 2007 treatment guidelines from the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) for the management of Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection outlined specific indications for diagnosis and treatment. These indications include: 1. Active peptic ulcer disease (PUD), whether gastric or duodenal in origin. 2. A confirmed history of peptic ulcer disease that has not been previously treated for H. pylori. 3. Low-grade gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma. 4. Following endoscopic resection of early gastric cancer (EGC). Recommended First-Line Treatment for H. pylori: Several combinations of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), clarithromycin, and amoxicillin have received FDA approval for the treatment of H. pylori infection. A regimen consisting of PPI, clarithromycin, and metronidazole is not FDA-approved. However, the combination product Pylera, which includes bismuth subcitrate, tetracycline, and metronidazole, used alongside a PPI for 10 days, is an FDA-approved treatment regimen. Adjuvant Therapy in the Treatment of H. pylori: Emerging evidence suggests that certain probiotic strains, such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species, may exert an inhibitory effect on H. pylori. These probiotics may also help reduce the side effects associated with eradication therapies and improve patient compliance with treatment. Selection of First-Line Treatment: Diagnostic Testing: The American Journal of Gastroenterology guidelines recommend performing endoscopy to rule out peptic ulcer disease, esophagogastric malignancy, and other rare upper gastrointestinal tract diseases in the following scenarios: Dyspeptic patients over the age of 55. Dyspeptic patients with alarm features, such as: Gastrointestinal bleeding. Anemia. Early satiety. Unexplained weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight. Progressive dysphagia. Odynophagia. Persistent vomiting. A family history of gastrointestinal cancer. A history of esophagogastric malignancy. Previously documented peptic ulcer, lymphadenopathy, or an abdominal mass. Management Options for Patients Aged 55 or Younger Without Alarm Features: 1. A test-and-treat strategy using a validated noninvasive test, such as a urea breath test or stool antigen test, to detect H. pylori. If eradication is successful but symptoms persist, a trial of acid suppression therapy may be considered. This approach is preferable in populations with a moderate to high prevalence of H. pylori infection (≥10%). 2. An empirical trial of acid suppression therapy using a proton pump inhibitor for 4–8 weeks. This approach is preferable in populations with a low prevalence of H. pylori infection. Repeat endoscopy is not recommended once a definitive diagnosis of functional dyspepsia has been established, unless new symptoms or alarm features develop. Testing for H. pylori Eradication: Testing to confirm eradication of H. pylori is most accurate when performed at least four weeks after the completion of therapy.
